Kelling introduced a simple concept: if a window in a building is left unrepaired, soon every window gets smashed. In Web3, this model plays out even more brutally: instead of shattered glass, we deal with sloppy code, weak third-party vendors, and structural oversights.  When infrastructure leaves even a minor backdoor unpatched, attackers instantly turn it into a highway for systemic exploits. A prime example is the recent $518M in suspicious funds routed through Sky Protocol’s Peg Stability Module, where an unaddressed structural loophole allowing swaps from $USDC into $DAI/$USDS enabled hackers to easily bypass Circle blacklists.  We see the exact same pattern in operational safety. The Gnosis Pay data leak caused by a third-party card vendor instantly endangered physical addresses, IBANs, and linked on-chain wallets. Meanwhile, physical implants found in cold storage hardware supply chains prove that bad actors test "broken windows" across every layer-from smart contract logic to physical shipping.  The most dangerous threat to Web3 isn't an isolated bug, but a culture that normalizes negligence. When teams skimp on audits and weaponize "code is law" to excuse carelessness, the environment naturally breeds disaster. Unlike traditional finance, on-chain execution lacks chargebacks or insurance safety nets, making the cost of every broken window exponentially higher.  Ecosystem security relies on zero tolerance for minor flaws and prompt resolution of small issues. In Web3, a broken window isn't just cosmetic neglect-it is an open invitation for an exploit. I have so many theories as to why this is.   1) A learned helplessness in the rank and file, instituted over the past two decades by a bipartisan leadership style that dictated to members in a top down manner what they were going to do and enforced it punitively using campaign cash, committee seats, etc, as leverage.   2) At least on the R side, we have reached a critical mass of senators who have never seen a functioning Senate. They have no idea how powerful they actually are or how the Senate operated in the Before Times (not even that long ago! Like in the 90s and early 2000s!).  Current senators either don’t want to know and outsource that knowledge to staff who are disinclined to do anything with it, or are gaslit into believing they require permission to use their considerable privileges. (The latter point drives me absolutely bananas. What’s the point of being a senator if you have to ask Mother May I every single time you want to BE A SENATOR. No wonder they’re all leaving for different jobs.)  3) The Senate has completely atrophied as a problem solving institution. Usually when things get stuck there are bipartisan “gangs” that form to solve the issue, lead negotiations, or walk the Senate back from the brink. This doesn’t happen anymore largely because senators don’t feel they have individual agency. See points 1 and 2.   4) Also per the last point, the committees are too large, and senators are on too many, to allow them to focus on two or three things and become The Guy about That Thing.   5) The committees are also deferential to leadership in a way they didn’t used to be, and that lack of independence dulls vital skill sets because it relies on other people to chew your food for you.  6) The modern Senate will do nothing unless they have a predetermined outcome. How many times has “we don’t have 60” been used as an excuse to do nothing? The Senate is a majestic institution precisely BECAUSE it is designed to leverage uncertainty into consensus. You never know how things will actually end until you fight them to the floor and give issues a political process, force a negotiation, and don’t give up until you’ve come to a solution. The greatest causes in American history didn’t *begin* with 60 or 67 (former cloture threshold) votes. They ended there after massive exertion and process.
